title: DNS, TCP, TLS & the HTTP Request
objectives: Trace the full journey of an HTTPS request from URL to response
Explain the cost of DNS, TCP, and TLS handshakes in round trips
Choose connection, protocol, and TLS strategies for latency-sensitive systems
body:
# DNS, TCP, TLS & the HTTP Request

## The problem
You type `https://example.com/api/users` into a browser. Seconds later a JSON document appears. Between those two moments the browser must resolve a name, open a transport connection, negotiate encryption, and only then send the actual HTTP request. Every downstream decision about web performance and reliability depends on understanding this lifecycle.

## Step 1: DNS resolution
The browser needs an IP address for `example.com`:

- Check the OS and browser DNS caches first.
- Query the configured recursive resolver (your ISP, or 8.8.8.8 / 1.1.1.1).
- The resolver walks the hierarchy: root -> .com TLD -> authoritative nameserver.

Tradeoff: long DNS TTLs reduce lookups but slow failover; short TTLs do the opposite. Production TTLs are typically 60-300 seconds.

## Step 2: TCP connection
With an IP in hand, the browser opens a TCP connection using the three-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. That is one full round trip before any HTTP bytes can flow. HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one connection; HTTP/3 replaces TCP with QUIC over UDP and folds the transport handshake into TLS.

## Step 3: TLS handshake
For `https://`, client and server negotiate keys and verify the certificate chain:

1. ClientHello with supported cipher suites and SNI.
2. ServerHello plus the certificate chain.
3. Key agreement and Finished messages.

TLS 1.3 needs a single extra round trip (0-RTT resumption is possible, but early data is replayable).

## The full cost picture

```text
DNS lookup         1+ RTT on a cache miss
TCP handshake      1 RTT
TLS 1.3 handshake  1 RTT
HTTP request       1 RTT
```

A cold fetch of one small resource costs at least four round trips. This is why connection reuse, keep-alive, and CDN edges near users matter so much: they delete whole round trips, not milliseconds.

## Decision framework
- Global audience with a tight latency budget? -> terminate TLS at CDN edges.
- Flaky mobile networks? -> HTTP/3 with session resumption; accept 0-RTT only for idempotent requests.
- Service-to-service traffic? -> mTLS with short-lived certs and service-discovery DNS.

## Best practices
- Cache DNS results, but keep TTLs low enough that failover completes in minutes.
- Always reuse connections (keep-alive); handshake cost dominates small requests.
- Prefer TLS 1.3 and disable TLS 1.0/1.1.
- Measure with `curl -w` so you can separate DNS, connect, TLS, and TTFB costs.

## Common mistakes
- Blaming the server for slow pages when DNS or TLS setup is the real cost.
- Setting a 1-day DNS TTL, then watching a failover take a day.
- Opening a fresh HTTP client per request in scripts instead of reusing one connection.
- Using TLS 0-RTT for non-idempotent requests; replayed early data can double-charge a payment.

examples.name: curl-timings.sh
examples.code:
# Measure each phase of the request lifecycle
curl -so /dev/null -w "dns=%{time_namelookup} tcp=%{time_connect} tls=%{time_appconnect} ttfb=%{time_starttransfer} total=%{time_total}\n" https://example.com

# Example output:
# dns=0.031 tcp=0.062 tls=0.124 ttfb=0.165 total=0.166

exercise.prompt: A browser fetches a small resource over HTTPS. rttMs is 40. The first fetch is cold (DNS cache miss, fresh connection, TLS 1.3); the second reuses the same keep-alive connection. Compute coldMs and warmMs so the preview shows both totals.
hints: Count the round trips: DNS (cache miss), TCP, TLS 1.3, then the HTTP exchange.
Each round trip costs rttMs; a warm keep-alive connection skips DNS, TCP, and TLS.
Cold is 4 x rttMs, warm is 1 x rttMs.

questions.prompt: How many round trips does a cold HTTPS fetch (DNS cache miss, TLS 1.3) need before the HTTP request/response completes?
questions.explanation: DNS lookup, TCP handshake, TLS 1.3 handshake, and the HTTP exchange each cost about one round trip: four in total.

questions.prompt: Which change most directly removes connection-setup round trips for repeat visits?
questions.explanation: QUIC combines transport and crypto handshakes and supports resumption, cutting setup round trips; DNS TTLs only affect name lookups.

questions.prompt: Why can TLS 1.3 0-RTT early data be dangerous?
options: It can be replayed by an attacker
questions.explanation: 0-RTT data is sent before fresh server input, so captured early data can be replayed; only idempotent requests should use it.
